text: Has a malware scanner actually identified any threats, let alone a threat that you can be certain came from PyPI? It feels as if you’re jumping to conclusions to immediately assume that PyPI is distributing malware. It seems likely that there are a lot of other possible explanations here.
author: duncathan

text:
I think @duncathan covered the biggest part here already but I will just add that there is plenty of security work that happens with PyPI such as Malware Reporting Evolved - The Python Package Index Blog already along with improvements that have been in various discussions like Pre-Pep: Staged Releases separated from PEP-694 which was moved to amendments to PEP 694.
If you want to check exactly what is in version of a package you are about to install to have more peace of mind you can use https://inspector.pypi.io/ to be able to inspect the contents of artifacts.
author: cjames23

text:
PyPi does ‘distribute’ malware, as you can verify with a quick internet search. See their own blog for example; Incident Report: LiteLLM/Telnyx supply-chain attacks, with guidance - The Python Package Index Blog
One cannot reasonably inspect the content of all artifacts they use, nor can one expect to recognise malware even if they do inspect it. There is peace of mind in knowing that security researchers have access to these artifacts.
But PyPi is doing their best, and their model is fundamentally incompatible with perfect safety. It’s a platform where anyone can publish code, and anyone can download it. I think that is valuable to have. Automated malware scanning cannot work perfectly. There will be false-positives and false-negatives. Perhaps there is also a place for a more ‘curated’ collection of Python libraries, but that’s not what PyPi is.
